newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Henkel moves closer to Loctite takeover.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Henkel moves closer to Loctite takeover.

text.p: Shares in German consumer products group Henkel KGaA rose on Monday after it said it was planning a 1.7 billion mark takeover bid for the U.S. adhesives group Loctite.

A spokesman for Henkel said it would use debt to finance the bid and said there would be no rights issue to cover the costs of the bid for Loctite, of which Henkel already owns 35 percent. Earlier, the group said it had offered to pay about $56 per share.
Henkel said it viewed its current stake in Loctite as a permanent investment and did not aim to sell it.
In a mandatory statement, Henkel said it expected to pay about 1.7 billion marks for the remaining 65 percent of Loctite.

Late on Monday afternoon, Loctite said it would review the Henkel proposal. "The company, its board of directors and management and their various advisers, will obviously review this proposal to determine the proper response," it said.

News of the takeover bid gave Henkel shares a lift on the German stock exchange. Dealers said they liked the news of the takeover bid, and Henkel preference shares ended bourse trade on the German DAX index at 68.70 marks, up 1.20 marks.
But the reaction from some analysts was less upbeat, and credit rating agency Standard & Poor's put the company on CreditWatch with negative implications on Monday afternoon.
S&P currently has AA minus senior unsecured and A1 plus commercial paper ratings for Henkel.
"About $160 million rated debt is affected," S&P said in a statement. The agency said the move would reinforce Henkel's global number one position in industrial and consumer adhesives.

But a 1.7 billion mark acquisition if debt-financed would double Henkel's debt, and S&P estimated operating profit net interest coverage could deteriorate from around five times in 1995 to three times next year on a proforma basis in 1997.

"There are some negative points. Since 1992, earnings have been somewhat stagnant at Loctite. 1996 was a good year for adhesives, but Loctite didn't share in the success," said one Frankfurt chemical-sector analyst.
"However, if they show they can improve it, then there is positive potential there," he said. "It also looks like good value, and I don't think it will be earnings diluting."
Henkel said its managing director Hans-Dietrich Winkhaus had met Loctite's president and chief executive, David Freeman, over the weekend and informed him of the bid proposal.
"Henkel offered to start talks with Loctite aimed at a swift and friendly takeover," the statement said.
The group said it had told Loctite it might decide to make a public takeover bid if the talks failed to make progress or floundered.
